stories.title: OpenWrt One – Open Hardware Router
stories.blurb: The OpenWrt project has released its first official reference hardware router — fully open-source, from firmware to schematics. For anyone serious about network privacy and avoiding black-box firmware, this is the gold standard. It's also a tangible win for open hardware as a movement.

stories.title: GLM 5.2 and the coming AI margin collapse
stories.blurb: China's GLM 5.2 is matching frontier model quality at a fraction of the cost, and this post argues it's the opening salvo in a race to zero on AI inference margins. If you're building AI-powered products, the economics of your stack are about to shift dramatically. Required reading for anyone with an API bill.

stories.title: A global workspace in language models
stories.blurb: Anthropic researchers find evidence of a "global workspace" mechanism inside LLMs — a bottleneck layer where verbalizable representations converge, mirroring a prominent theory of human consciousness. It's a rare piece of mechanistic interpretability research that has genuine philosophical weight. Claude users will want to understand how their tool actually works.

stories.title: Fable turned reMarkable into Tom Riddle's diary from Harry Potter
stories.blurb: This open-source project uses Fable (an AI agent framework) to make a reMarkable tablet respond to your handwriting as if it were possessed — the AI reads what you write and responds in the same notebook. Wildly creative intersection of hardware hacking and LLM agents. The GitHub repo is surprisingly approachable.

stories.title: CoMaps – FOSS Offline Maps
stories.blurb: CoMaps is a fully offline, open-source maps app — a privacy-respecting alternative to Google Maps that doesn't phone home. It works on both iOS and Android, stores all map data locally, and has no ads or tracking. If you've been looking for a Maps.me or OsmAnd alternative, this is it.

stories.title: Pruning RAG context down to what the answer actually needs
stories.blurb: Kapa's engineering team shares their production technique for stripping RAG context down to only the sentences that actually matter for a given query. Smaller context = cheaper, faster, and often more accurate responses. This is the kind of practical, battle-tested optimization you can apply to your own AI pipelines today.

stories.title: OfficeCLI: Office suite for AI agents to read and edit Microsoft Office files
stories.blurb: A CLI tool that lets AI agents (like Claude Code) read, write, and manipulate Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files without needing Office installed. This fills a real gap in agentic workflows where the world is still full of .docx and .xlsx files. Drop it into your MCP setup and automate the Office paperwork.

stories.title: NSA and IETF: Fairness
stories.blurb: DJB (Daniel J. Bernstein, author of Curve25519 and NaCl) writes a detailed, pointed critique of NSA influence over IETF cryptography standardization processes. If you care about the integrity of the protocols underpinning the internet, this is a sobering and technically grounded read from one of the most credible voices in the field.

stories.title: Januscape: Guest-to-Host Escape in KVM/x86 [CVE-2026-53359]
stories.blurb: A working guest-to-host escape exploit for KVM/x86 virtualization has been published. This is a critical class of vulnerability — any cloud workload or dev environment relying on KVM-based VMs needs to assess exposure. Full writeup and PoC are on GitHub.

stories.title: Ternlight – 7 MB embedding model that runs in browser (WASM)
stories.blurb: A 7 MB text embedding model that runs entirely in the browser via WASM — no server, no API key, no data leaving the device. The live demo is genuinely impressive. This is a game-changer for building privacy-preserving semantic search or note-linking features (hello, Obsidian plugin authors).

stories.title: I set up Claude Code the way Anthropic now recommends, and the sub-agents-spawning-sub-agents trick changed how I work
stories.blurb: A hands-on walkthrough of Anthropic's recommended Claude Code configuration, with focus on the sub-agent orchestration pattern where Claude spawns specialized child agents for parallel tasks. Directly relevant for anyone using Claude Code in their daily dev workflow. The multi-agent approach is reportedly a step-change in throughput for complex coding tasks.

stories.title: The Anti-Slop Frontend Framework
stories.blurb: Taste Skill is an open-source collection of "skill files" you feed to AI coding agents to stop them from generating generic, cookie-cutter UI. Think of it as a style guide your AI actually follows. Directly relevant for Angular/TypeScript devs tired of GPT-generated sludge UIs.

stories.title: Price per 1M tokens is meaningless | Jan Iłowski
stories.blurb: A sharp takedown of the industry's obsession with $/1M token pricing — the author shows why it's a misleading metric that ignores context window efficiency, output quality, and task completion rate. If you're comparing LLMs for a production product, this reframes the whole analysis.

stories.title: Postgres Is Enough
stories.blurb: A curated directory showing how PostgreSQL extensions and built-in features can replace Redis, Elasticsearch, Kafka, MongoDB, and more. It's a useful reference for .NET/full-stack developers who want to shrink their infrastructure footprint. Sometimes the boring database is the best architecture.

stories.title: The Full Stack of Terminals Explained: Terminal, Shell, TTY, Console, POSIX, ANSI Escapes, PTYs, Raw/Canonical Modes
stories.byline: Pinboard Popular · tagged: terminal, shell, tty, console, posix, ansi
stories.blurb: A comprehensive deep-dive that finally explains all the overlapping jargon around terminals — from what a TTY actually is to how PTYs work and the difference between raw and canonical mode. If you build CLI tools or work in the terminal daily, this is the reference you've been missing. Bookmark it.

stories.title: Michael Tsai - Blog - Backblaze No Longer Backs Up Dropbox
stories.byline: Pinboard Popular · tagged: 2026, mjtsai, backblaze, apps, software, mac, macos, backup, dropbox
stories.blurb: Backblaze quietly stopped backing up Dropbox folders — and worse, silently discarded existing Dropbox backups without warning. Michael Tsai's roundup collects user reports and commentary. macOS users relying on Backblaze for full-disk backup need to audit their setup immediately.

stories.title: Daring Fireball: Apple Should Eliminate the App Icon 'Squircle Jail'
stories.blurb: John Gruber argues Apple should let iOS app icons break free from the forced squircle mask and allow designers full control over icon shape, as macOS already does. It's a perennial debate, but the argument is sharpened by visionOS precedent. Anyone who cares about Apple design aesthetics will have opinions.

stories.title: Dark mode with web standards
stories.byline: Pinboard Popular · tagged: to_share, css-dark-mode, prefers-color-scheme-guide, javascript-toggle, svg-iframes-example, container-queries-tool
stories.blurb: A practical, modern guide to implementing dark mode using only web standards — `prefers-color-scheme`, `color-scheme`, and the new `light-dark()` CSS function — with a JS toggle that respects user preference. No frameworks, no libraries. Directly applicable for any Angular or web project.

stories.title: GitHub - can1357/pon: Python 3.14, compiled to metal — JIT & AoT native compiler and runtime in Rust
stories.blurb: Pon is an ambitious Python-to-native compiler written in Rust, using Cranelift as its backend, the Ruff parser, and a custom GC called Green Tea. It claims byte-exact differential testing against CPython. Early-stage but technically fascinating — the kind of project that could reshape Python's performance story if it matures.

stories.title: Show HN: Fast, native Mac file manager (filters, fuzzy find, 9 MB, no Electron)
stories.blurb: Whim is a native macOS file manager that weighs just 9 MB, offers fuzzy find, and has zero Electron overhead — a rare thing in 2026. Early-stage and low-scoring on HN, but exactly the kind of nimble native Mac utility our reader appreciates. Worth a look if Finder's limitations frustrate you.
